script.opening: "Doctor, this letter's frightened the life out of me. It says I've got an aneurysm on my aorta, 4.3 centimetres. My brother died when his aorta burst — just dropped dead — so I'm convinced mine's going to do the same any minute. Do I need an operation right now? Should I stop driving, stop lifting, stop everything? I've been too scared to even go for a walk."

facts.text: If asked: you had an ultrasound of your tummy for a gallstone check, and the report mentioned "abdominal aortic aneurysm 4.3 cm". The letter came on Monday asking you to see the GP. Nobody has explained it.
None. No tummy or back pain, no pulsing lump you have noticed, no fainting, no breathlessness, no chest pain. You feel physically well.

facts.topic: What has changed since the letter
facts.text: You have barely slept for four nights. You have stopped your daily walk with the dog, stopped lifting your grandson and won't drive "in case it goes at the wheel".
High blood pressure (amlodipine), high cholesterol — "they offered me a statin, I didn't fancy it". No allergies. Last BP at the nurse: "about 150 over 90".
15 a day for 50 years. "I've cut down a bit since the letter, to be honest." You have tried patches before.
69, retired bus mechanic, married to Sue, three grandchildren. Drinks a few pints at the weekend.
Your older brother Jim "dropped dead" at 72, five years ago, at home. The post-mortem said a burst aorta. "Nobody knew he had anything."

Very frightened, talking quickly, convinced you are a ticking bomb. If the doctor gives you clear, simple facts (small, low risk at this size, checked by scans, operation only if it grows much bigger), visibly relax and say: "So I can walk the dog?" Become interested once smoking is framed as something you can actually do to help. If they say "don't worry" without facts, stay frightened: "That's what they told Jim."

ice.ideas: "It's going to burst any minute, like Jim's did."
ice.concerns: "I keep thinking I'll drop dead in front of Sue or the grandkids."
ice.expectations: "Do I need an operation now? Should I stop everything?" You want honest facts and to know what you can do.

cues: "My brother died when his burst." — say in the opening.
"I've been too scared to even go for a walk." — say in the opening.
"I've cut down on the cigs since the letter." — say when lifestyle comes up.

checkpoints.text: Explains accurately that a 4.3 cm AAA is SMALL and LOW rupture-risk, managed by SURVEILLANCE (regular ultrasound) and risk-factor modification — NOT emergency surgery — and that repair is generally considered only at ~5.5 cm, rapid growth (>1 cm/year), or if symptomatic

Refers to the regional vascular service to be seen within 12 weeks of diagnosis (NICE NG156: 3.0–5.4 cm; 5.5 cm or more within 2 weeks; symptomatic = emergency) and sets out the SURVEILLANCE plan clearly (ultrasound every 12 months at 3.0–4.4 cm, every 3 months at 4.5–5.4 cm — NHS AAA Screening Programme, adopted by NG156) and what the thresholds for repair are, so the patient understands the watch-and-monitor logic

Frames RISK-FACTOR modification as empowering and effective: smoking cessation (a major modifiable factor, consistently linked to faster growth and higher rupture rates — Sweeting et al., Br J Surg 2012; stop-smoking support per NICE NG209) and blood-pressure control (NICE NG136), plus statin/cardiovascular risk (NICE NG238) — framing BP and lipids as protecting his heart and circulation overall rather than claiming they shrink the aneurysm — giving him genuine agency rather than helplessness

Gives the genuine RED FLAGS that would be an emergency: sudden severe abdominal/back/flank pain, collapse/syncope, a painful pulsatile mass → 999 (possible rupture) — distinguishing these from his current asymptomatic, low-risk state

Gives permission to LIVE NORMALLY: normal activity and exercise are encouraged, not forbidden; corrects the "stop everything" misconception (reasonable to avoid only very heavy isometric straining if advised, but not normal life/walking)
Responds to the distress and sleeplessness first, dismantles the brother-driven catastrophe with empathy and accurate information, and replaces dread with an accurate, empowering narrative
Acknowledges the harm of a cold letter without a conversation, validates the fear given the family history, and reassures without either minimising or feeding the catastrophe

Safety-nets and follows up: the surveillance schedule, rupture red flags → 999, smoking-cessation and BP support, permission to resume normal life, and a follow-up that leaves him reassured and engaged rather than paralysed by fear

worked.txt: "I’m so sorry that letter has terrified you and stolen your sleep — let me put this in proportion straightaway, because the reality is far less frightening than it feels. Yes, you have a small bulge on the main blood vessel — an aneurysm — but at 4.3 centimetres it is SMALL, and the risk of it bursting at this size is LOW. You do not need an emergency operation, and it is not about to go ‘any minute’."

"I know your brother died of this, and that’s exactly why this landed so hard — your mind has written you into his story. But his was almost certainly far larger by the time it ruptured. Yours has been found early and small, which is the whole point of finding it: it puts you in a completely different, much safer position than he was in."

"So what we DO is refer you to the vascular specialists — they should see you within 12 weeks — and keep an eye on it with a simple ultrasound scan, about once a year at this size. Most small aneurysms grow very slowly, if at all. Only if it grew to around 5.5 centimetres, or grew quickly, would we talk about a planned repair — and that’s a controlled, planned operation, nothing like an emergency. You’re a long way from that."

"Here’s the empowering bit: you are NOT helpless. The single best thing you can do for the aneurysm is to stop smoking — smoking is linked to these growing faster — and I’ll help you. Keeping your blood pressure and cholesterol controlled protects your heart and circulation too. So instead of sitting in fear, you’ve got real things you can DO that tip the odds in your favour."

"And please — go back to your life. Walk, garden, drive, enjoy yourself. Stopping everything won’t protect you and is robbing you of living. Normal activity and exercise are actually GOOD for you here. You don’t need to wrap yourself in cotton wool."

"One thing to know, just in case — not to scare you, but so you’re informed: if you ever got sudden severe pain in your tummy or back, or felt faint or collapsed, that’s a 999 emergency. That’s the only scenario to act on urgently, and it’s not where you are. Otherwise: I’ll send the vascular referral today, set up your monitoring scans, help you with the smoking, and see you to go through it all. Please, sleep tonight — this is small, watched, and largely in your hands."

f.learning: A 4.3 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is SMALL and LOW rupture-risk — managed by SURVEILLANCE (periodic ultrasound) and risk-factor modification, NOT emergency surgery; repair is generally considered only at ~5.5 cm, rapid growth (>1 cm/year), or if symptomatic. The consultation is largely RISK COMMUNICATION: a cold letter and a brother’s death from a ruptured aorta have produced catastrophic certainty and total activity avoidance. Dismantle it accurately (small, low-risk, found early, monitored), refer to the regional vascular service to be seen within 12 weeks (NICE NG156, 2020), set out the surveillance plan and the repair thresholds, and — crucially — frame risk-factor modification (above all smoking cessation, linked to growth and rupture; plus BP/cholesterol control for his overall cardiovascular risk) as empowering and effective, giving agency rather than helplessness. Give explicit permission to live normally (normal activity/exercise encouraged), correcting the "stop everything" misconception, and give the genuine rupture red flags (sudden severe abdominal/back/flank pain, collapse → 999) to act on. Respond to the distress first, validate the family-history fear, and reassure without minimising or feeding the catastrophe. What WOULD be an emergency: sudden severe abdominal/back/flank pain, a pulsatile abdominal mass with pain, collapse/syncope, or shock — suggesting rupture or symptomatic AAA (a surgical emergency, 999). He is currently asymptomatic — the message is surveillance now, but know-and-act on these red flags.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG156 (Abdominal aortic aneurysm, 2020) · NHS AAA Screening Programme surveillance guidance (GOV.UK) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (2025) · NICE NG209 (Tobacco, 2021) · NICE NG136 (Hypertension, 2019) · NICE NG238 (Cardiovascular risk and lipids, 2023)
knowledge.summary: A 4.3 cm aneurysm is small. It needs referral to the regional vascular service, regular ultrasound surveillance and risk-factor control — not emergency surgery and not a life on hold.

points.t: NHS AAA Screening Programme: small 3.0–4.4 cm (ultrasound every 12 months), medium 4.5–5.4 cm (every 3 months), large 5.5 cm or more. NICE NG156 recommends surveillance at the same frequency as the screening programme.

NICE NG156: refer an AAA of 3.0–5.4 cm to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks of diagnosis; 5.5 cm or larger within 2 weeks. A symptomatic aneurysm needs emergency assessment whatever its size.

Repair is generally considered for an asymptomatic AAA of 5.5 cm or more, or one that grows by more than 1 cm in a year (NICE NG156; screening programme referral criteria). It is then a planned operation, not an emergency.

Stopping smoking is the most important modifiable step for an aneurysm: offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209). Keep blood pressure to target (NICE NG136) and review lipid management (NICE NG238) to reduce his overall cardiovascular risk.

DVLA: Group 1 (car) drivers need to notify only at 6.0 cm or more, and must not drive at 6.5 cm or more. Group 2 (lorry, bus) drivers must notify at any size and must not drive at 5.5 cm or more. Normal walking and day-to-day activity do not need to stop.
Sudden severe abdominal, back or flank pain, collapse or feeling faint in someone with a known AAA is a 999 emergency.

Symptomatic versus asymptomatic AAA; small versus larger aneurysm; his fear versus the actual risk.

Idea (about to burst, needs an operation); concern (dying like his brother); expectation (emergency surgery, stop all activity).

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Castle, I’m Dr Lee. Can I just check your date of birth and that you’re somewhere you can talk? … Thank you. I can see you’ve had the scan letter. How are you doing with it?
model.why: Checks identity on video, then opens with his experience, not the number

model.text: Frightened the life out of me. Four point three centimetres. My brother died when his aorta burst — just dropped. I’ve not slept. Do I need an operation now? Should I stop driving, lifting, everything? I’ve not even been out for a walk.

I’m really sorry — that letter landed on top of something very painful. I want to answer every one of those questions. Can I first ask a few things so the answers fit you, and then we’ll make a plan together?
model.why: Acknowledges distress and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Please. I just want to know where I stand.
First, the important one: have you had any pain in your tummy, back or side, or any dizzy spells or blackouts?
model.why: Rules out a symptomatic aneurysm first

model.text: No. Nothing. I feel completely normal — that’s what’s so frightening.
That’s actually very good news, and I’ll explain why. Can you tell me about your brother — what happened?
He was fine one day, gone the next. Collapsed at home. They said his aorta burst. I keep picturing it happening to me.
That must be a terrible thing to carry, and it makes complete sense this letter has brought it all back. Did anyone tell you how big his was, or whether it had been found before?
model.why: Validates, then gently tests the comparison he is making

model.text: I don’t know. He never said anything about having one.
Thank you. And how are the cigarettes going — you said you were trying to stop?
model.why: Explores the main modifiable risk factor

model.text: I’d cut right down. Honestly, since the letter it’s gone back up. Nerves.
Understandable. And the driving you mentioned — is that just your car, or do you drive a lorry or bus at all?
model.why: Clarifies licence group before giving DVLA advice

model.text: Just the car.

Right — let me put this in proportion, because the reality is much less frightening than it feels. At 4.3 centimetres your aneurysm is in the small group. The risk of it bursting at this size is low. You don’t need an emergency operation, and it isn’t about to go any minute.
model.why: Accurate reassurance: small AAA, low risk, no emergency surgery

model.text: But my brother’s…

Many people whose aneurysm bursts never knew they had one, so it was never measured or watched. Yours has been found while it’s small, and that puts you in a very different position. The whole point of finding it is so we can keep an eye on it.
model.why: Dismantles the brother comparison with facts and empathy

model.text: So what actually happens now?

I’ll refer you to the vascular team, who should see you within about 12 weeks. They’ll arrange an ultrasound scan every year to measure it. Many small ones grow slowly. Only if it reached about 5.5 centimetres, or grew quickly, would they talk about a planned repair — a booked operation, nothing like an emergency.
model.why: Explains NG156 referral, surveillance interval and repair thresholds

model.text: Every year? That’s it?
That’s it, unless it changes. And on driving: for a car licence you don’t need to tell the DVLA at this size. You can keep driving.

Here’s the part I most want you to hear: you’re not helpless. Stopping smoking is the single most useful thing you can do for an aneurysm. Keeping your blood pressure and cholesterol well controlled protects your heart and circulation too. What would help you most with the smoking right now?
model.why: Frames risk-factor change as agency and invites his input

model.text: Maybe I need proper help this time.

Then let’s refer you to the stop-smoking service — they give you medication and weekly support, and it works much better than willpower alone. I’ll also check your blood pressure and cholesterol and review your tablets.
model.why: Offers evidence-based cessation support and CV risk review

model.text: And walking? The garden?

Please go back to both. Walking is good for you. Normal life doesn’t make an aneurysm burst — staying indoors frightened just takes your life away from you. If the vascular team want you to avoid anything very heavy, they’ll tell you.
model.why: Gives explicit permission to resume normal activity

model.text: (Exhales.) I’ve just been sat in the chair since that letter came.

One thing to know, just so you’re informed and not to worry you: if you ever had sudden severe pain in your tummy, back or side, or felt faint or collapsed, that’s a 999 call and you tell them you have an aneurysm. That’s the only thing to act on urgently, and it isn’t where you are now.
model.why: Specific rupture red flags without feeding the fear

model.text: Okay. Sudden bad pain or collapse, 999.
Exactly. Can you tell me in your own words what you’ll say if someone asks what the doctor said today?
It’s small, they’ll scan it every year, no operation now, stop smoking, and I can go for a walk.
Perfect. I’ll see you in a month with your blood pressure and to see how the smoking’s going — sooner if you’re struggling with the worry. How are you feeling now?
model.why: Defined follow-up and checks the emotional outcome

model.text: Much better. I might actually sleep tonight.

social.t: His brother’s sudden death has shaped how he hears the word “aneurysm”. Stopping all activity and losing sleep are signs of how much it has taken over.
The letter has pushed his smoking back up. Support rather than blame.

legal.t: Group 1: notify DVLA at 6.0 cm or more; must not drive at 6.5 cm or more. Group 2: notify at any size; must not drive at 5.5 cm or more. At 4.3 cm with a car licence he can drive without notifying.

professional.t: A significant result sent by letter without a conversation can cause harm. Offer a timely discussion when results carry emotional weight, and reflect on the practice’s results process (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: communicate effectively).
Make sure the NICE NG156 vascular referral is sent and he is enrolled in surveillance, so he is not lost to follow-up.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service; the Circulation Foundation for patient information on aneurysms; bereavement support if the brother’s death remains raw.

Not sleeping, stopped walking and daily activities
Smoking back up since the letter; car driver
ice: Idea: the aneurysm could burst any minute and needs an operation now
Concern: dying the way his brother did
Expectation: emergency surgery and being told to stop everything

playbook.diagnosis: Be precise: “At 4.3 centimetres this is a small aneurysm. The risk of it bursting at this size is low. It needs watching with a yearly scan, not an operation.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of a slightly stretched section of garden hose. At this size it’s not near bursting. We measure it every year, and if it ever stretched to the size where it could become a problem, the surgeons would reinforce it as a planned job.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been picturing what happened to your brother. Yours has been found early and small, and it will be watched — and that’s what makes the difference.”
management.psychosocial: Give permission to walk and garden again; offer stop-smoking support without blame; follow up the anxiety and consider bereavement support.
sharedPlan: Refer to regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks (NICE NG156); yearly ultrasound surveillance
Stop-smoking service referral (NICE NG209); review BP (NICE NG136) and lipids (NICE NG238)
Normal activity and car driving continue; no need to notify DVLA at this size
safetyNet: Sudden severe abdominal, back or flank pain, feeling faint or collapse — 999 and say he has an aneurysm
Review in a month; earlier if the worry is not settling

pitfalls.intro: This is a risk-communication station. The clinical facts are simple; candidates fail by reassuring without evidence, by adding restrictions that feed the fear, or by forgetting that a small aneurysm still needs a referral and a plan.

items.fail: Launching into reassurance without first asking about pain or collapse.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” A symptomatic aneurysm is an emergency at any size.
items.fix: Ask first: any tummy, back or side pain, dizziness or blackouts? Then reassure.

items.fail: Telling him the practice will just scan it again next year.
items.why: NICE NG156 recommends referral to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks, for an AAA of 3.0–5.4 cm.
items.fix: Name the referral, the yearly scan and the repair thresholds in plain words.

items.fail: Telling him to stop driving or tell the DVLA, or not addressing driving at all.
items.why: Incorrect DVLA advice is a Tasks error and adds harm. At 4.3 cm a car driver need not notify.
items.fix: Check his licence group first, then give the correct answer.

items.fail: Not asking about the brother, or saying “that won’t happen to you”.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The brother’s death is the whole of his fear; false promises lose trust.
items.fix: Ask what happened, then use it: an aneurysm found early and watched is in a different position from one nobody knew about.

items.fail: Lecturing about smoking after he admits it has gone up.
items.why: Shame after a relapse lowers the chance he engages with support.
items.fix: Normalise the relapse and offer the stop-smoking service as a way of taking control.

items.fail: Closing with “any questions?” and no check that the reassurance has landed.
items.why: Frightened patients remember the fear, not the facts. Unchecked understanding is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back — “What will you say about today?” — plus the 999 red flags and a booked review.

timeMap.d: He arrives with a list of frightened questions. Let him finish and promise to answer every one.
Pain or collapse first. Then the brother’s story, the smoking relapse and his licence group.
Small, low risk, found early. Vascular referral within 12 weeks, yearly scans, repair only around 5.5 cm or rapid growth. Car driving continues.
Stop-smoking service, BP and cholesterol. Explicit permission to walk and garden again.
Sudden severe pain or collapse — 999. Teach-back. Review in a month.

wordPics.fail: Either tells him not to worry without explaining why, or feeds the fear by listing what could go wrong; no symptom check; no vascular referral or surveillance plan; wrong or no advice on driving and activity; brother never mentioned.
wordPics.pass: Checks for symptoms; explains small size and low risk; refers for surveillance; advises stopping smoking; gives rupture red flags; acknowledges the brother’s death.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains why an aneurysm found early and watched is in a different position from one that ruptures unrecognised; gives the NG156 referral timeframe, yearly scans and repair thresholds in plain words; correct DVLA advice after checking his licence; frames smoking cessation as control; gives explicit permission to live normally; teach-back and follow-up for the anxiety.

avoid.dont: "It’s only small, there’s really nothing to worry about."
avoid.instead: "At this size the risk is low, and here is exactly how we’ll keep it that way."
avoid.why: Dismissive reassurance ignores his brother’s death and does not give him a plan to trust.

avoid.dont: "Avoid heavy lifting, straining and stressful situations for now."
avoid.instead: "Please go back to walking and the garden. If the vascular team want you to avoid anything, they’ll tell you."
avoid.why: Vague restrictions confirm the catastrophe and keep him housebound.

avoid.dont: "You really must stop smoking or it will get bigger."
avoid.instead: "Stopping smoking is the most useful thing you can do for it — shall we get you proper help this time?"
avoid.why: A threat after a relapse drives shame; an offer of support gives him control.

One thing to know, just so you’re informed and not to worry you: if you ever had sudden severe pain in your tummy, back or side, or felt faint or collapsed, that’s a 999 call and you tell them you have an aneurysm. That’s the only thing to act on urgently, and it isn’t where you are now.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific rupture red flags without feeding the fear

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Sudden bad pain or collapse, 999.
Exactly. Can you tell me in your own words what you’ll say if someone asks what the doctor said today?
It’s small, they’ll scan it every year, no operation now, stop smoking, and I can go for a walk.
Perfect. I’ll see you in a month with your blood pressure and to see how the smoking’s going — sooner if you’re struggling with the worry. How are you feeling now?
SCA_MODELS.why: Defined follow-up and checks the emotional outcome

SCA_MODELS.text: Much better. I might actually sleep tonight.

SCA_STEM.name: Brian Castle
SCA_STEM.recent: Ultrasound report received: abdominal aortic aneurysm, maximum diameter 4.3 cm. Patient has had the result letter. Family history: brother died of a ruptured aorta.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment requested: “worried sick about the aneurysm letter”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG156 (Abdominal aortic aneurysm, 2020) · NHS AAA Screening Programme surveillance guidance (GOV.UK) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (2025) · NICE NG209 (Tobacco, 2021) · NICE NG136 (Hypertension, 2019) · NICE NG238 (Cardiovascular risk and lipids, 2023)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 4.3 cm aneurysm is small. It needs referral to the regional vascular service, regular ultrasound surveillance and risk-factor control — not emergency surgery and not a life on hold.

points.t: NHS AAA Screening Programme: small 3.0–4.4 cm (ultrasound every 12 months), medium 4.5–5.4 cm (every 3 months), large 5.5 cm or more. NICE NG156 recommends surveillance at the same frequency as the screening programme.

NICE NG156: refer an AAA of 3.0–5.4 cm to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks of diagnosis; 5.5 cm or larger within 2 weeks. A symptomatic aneurysm needs emergency assessment whatever its size.

Repair is generally considered for an asymptomatic AAA of 5.5 cm or more, or one that grows by more than 1 cm in a year (NICE NG156; screening programme referral criteria). It is then a planned operation, not an emergency.

Stopping smoking is the most important modifiable step for an aneurysm: offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209). Keep blood pressure to target (NICE NG136) and review lipid management (NICE NG238) to reduce his overall cardiovascular risk.

DVLA: Group 1 (car) drivers need to notify only at 6.0 cm or more, and must not drive at 6.5 cm or more. Group 2 (lorry, bus) drivers must notify at any size and must not drive at 5.5 cm or more. Normal walking and day-to-day activity do not need to stop.
Sudden severe abdominal, back or flank pain, collapse or feeling faint in someone with a known AAA is a 999 emergency.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Opened with how he is coping with the letter rather than the measurement; let him voice all his questions.
Explored the lost week (not sleeping, not walking), his smoking and his driving licence group.
Followed the brother’s death as the central cue, and the smoking relapse since the letter.
Idea (about to burst, needs an operation); concern (dying like his brother); expectation (emergency surgery, stop all activity).
Symptom screen for pain or collapse; BP and lipid review; referral to vascular service for surveillance ultrasound.
Symptomatic versus asymptomatic AAA; small versus larger aneurysm; his fear versus the actual risk.
Ruled out current symptoms first and gave explicit rupture red flags with 999.
Named it as a small aneurysm with low rupture risk and explained the size thresholds for repair.
Referral to be seen within 12 weeks (NICE NG156), annual ultrasound, stop-smoking service, permission to resume walking and driving.
Hypertension and cholesterol control reviewed; smoking relapse addressed; DVLA Group 1 advice given correctly.
Teach-back, rupture red flags, review in a month and an open door for the anxiety.

social.t: His brother’s sudden death has shaped how he hears the word “aneurysm”. Stopping all activity and losing sleep are signs of how much it has taken over.
The letter has pushed his smoking back up. Support rather than blame.

legal.t: Group 1: notify DVLA at 6.0 cm or more; must not drive at 6.5 cm or more. Group 2: notify at any size; must not drive at 5.5 cm or more. At 4.3 cm with a car licence he can drive without notifying.

professional.t: A significant result sent by letter without a conversation can cause harm. Offer a timely discussion when results carry emotional weight, and reflect on the practice’s results process (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: communicate effectively).
Make sure the NICE NG156 vascular referral is sent and he is enrolled in surveillance, so he is not lost to follow-up.

community.t: Local NHS stop-smoking service; the Circulation Foundation for patient information on aneurysms; bereavement support if the brother’s death remains raw.

redFlags: Abdominal, back or flank pain — a symptomatic AAA needs emergency assessment
psychosocial: Brother died suddenly of a ruptured aorta
Not sleeping, stopped walking and daily activities
Smoking back up since the letter; car driver
ice: Idea: the aneurysm could burst any minute and needs an operation now
Concern: dying the way his brother did
Expectation: emergency surgery and being told to stop everything

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be precise: “At 4.3 centimetres this is a small aneurysm. The risk of it bursting at this size is low. It needs watching with a yearly scan, not an operation.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a slightly stretched section of garden hose. At this size it’s not near bursting. We measure it every year, and if it ever stretched to the size where it could become a problem, the surgeons would reinforce it as a planned job.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been picturing what happened to your brother. Yours has been found early and small, and it will be watched — and that’s what makes the difference.”
management.psychosocial: Give permission to walk and garden again; offer stop-smoking support without blame; follow up the anxiety and consider bereavement support.
sharedPlan: Refer to regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks (NICE NG156); yearly ultrasound surveillance
Stop-smoking service referral (NICE NG209); review BP (NICE NG136) and lipids (NICE NG238)
Normal activity and car driving continue; no need to notify DVLA at this size
safetyNet: Sudden severe abdominal, back or flank pain, feeling faint or collapse — 999 and say he has an aneurysm
Review in a month; earlier if the worry is not settling

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a risk-communication station. The clinical facts are simple; candidates fail by reassuring without evidence, by adding restrictions that feed the fear, or by forgetting that a small aneurysm still needs a referral and a plan.

items.fail: Launching into reassurance without first asking about pain or collapse.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” A symptomatic aneurysm is an emergency at any size.
items.fix: Ask first: any tummy, back or side pain, dizziness or blackouts? Then reassure.

items.fail: Telling him the practice will just scan it again next year.
items.why: NICE NG156 recommends referral to a regional vascular service, to be seen within 12 weeks, for an AAA of 3.0–5.4 cm.
items.fix: Name the referral, the yearly scan and the repair thresholds in plain words.

items.fail: Telling him to stop driving or tell the DVLA, or not addressing driving at all.
items.why: Incorrect DVLA advice is a Tasks error and adds harm. At 4.3 cm a car driver need not notify.
items.fix: Check his licence group first, then give the correct answer.

items.fail: Not asking about the brother, or saying “that won’t happen to you”.
items.why: “Does not respond to cues.” The brother’s death is the whole of his fear; false promises lose trust.
items.fix: Ask what happened, then use it: an aneurysm found early and watched is in a different position from one nobody knew about.

items.fail: Lecturing about smoking after he admits it has gone up.
items.why: Shame after a relapse lowers the chance he engages with support.
items.fix: Normalise the relapse and offer the stop-smoking service as a way of taking control.

items.fail: Closing with “any questions?” and no check that the reassurance has landed.
items.why: Frightened patients remember the fear, not the facts. Unchecked understanding is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Teach-back — “What will you say about today?” — plus the 999 red flags and a booked review.
